name: Trader test battery, version 3
models: Reported, as of Nov 2026: the Optiver, IMC and Citadel Securities test batteries. Number sequences, probability at speed, and likelihood ranking with intervals.
description: These are reported formats from the Optiver, IMC and Citadel Securities test batteries, as described by Nov 2026. There are three papers, each on its own clock. Sequences is 15 questions in 25 minutes, one at a time, with no skipping. Probability at speed is 15 questions in 30 minutes; you may move between them. Likelihood ranking and intervals is 10 questions in 10 minutes. Wrong answers score 0, and no calculator is allowed. Firms mix and rename these papers, so expect a different order on the day. This is version 3 of 3.

options.why: You added 0.00001. Each term adds the next digit on the end.
You rounded. Each term keeps every digit and adds one more.
You dropped the first digit. The digits only grow.

feedback.correct: Each term adds the next digit: 1, 2, 3, then 6.
feedback.generic: Look at the digits, not the size of the gaps.

explain.text: Each term writes one more digit of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 after the point. The fifth term has five digits, so the sixth is 0.123456. Check: the gaps 0.02, 0.003, 0.0004, 0.00005 continue with 0.000006.

items.title: Top and bottom
items.question: What comes next? $\tfrac13, \tfrac25, \tfrac37, \tfrac49, \tfrac{5}{11}$, ?

options.why: You raised the bottom by 1. It rises by 2.
You raised only the bottom. The top rises by 1 too.
You raised the top by 2. It rises by 1.

feedback.correct: The top counts up by 1 and the bottom by 2: $\tfrac{n}{2n + 1}$.
feedback.generic: Treat the tops and the bottoms as two sequences.

explain.text: The tops are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and the bottoms 3, 5, 7, 9, 11. So the next is $\tfrac{6}{13}$. Check: each term is $\tfrac{n}{2n + 1}$, and $n = 6$ gives $\tfrac{6}{13}$.

options.why: You counted on. 3 is not allowed: every digit is 1 or 2.
122 qualifies, but 121 comes first.
211 qualifies, but 121 and 122 come first.

feedback.correct: The numbers whose digits are all 1 or 2, in order.
feedback.generic: Which digits appear in the terms?

explain.text: Every term uses only the digits 1 and 2, listed in order. After 112 the next such number is 121. Check: 113 to 120 each contain a digit other than 1 or 2.

items.title: Square steps
items.question: What comes next? 2, 3, 7, 16, 32, ?

options.why: You repeated the last gap of 16. The gaps are 1, 4, 9, 16, then 25.
You doubled 32. The gaps are the square numbers.
You were one out. $32 + 25 = 57$.

feedback.correct: The gaps are the squares 1, 4, 9, 16, 25.
feedback.generic: Write down the gaps.

explain.text: The gaps are 1, 4, 9 and 16, the squares. The next gap is 25, so the next term is $32 + 25 = 57$. Check: $2 + (1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25) = 2 + 55 = 57$.

items.title: Prime steps
items.question: What comes next? 1, 3, 6, 11, 18, 29, ?

options.why: You repeated the last gap of 11. The gaps are primes, and 13 comes next.
You doubled 29. The gaps are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11.
You added 12. 12 is not prime.

feedback.correct: The gaps are the primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13.
feedback.generic: Write down the gaps.

explain.text: The gaps are 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11, the primes in order. The next prime is 13, so the next term is $29 + 13 = 42$. Check: $1 + (2 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 11 + 13) = 1 + 41 = 42$.

items.title: Last digits
items.question: What comes next? 1, 4, 9, 6, 5, 6, 9, ?

options.why: You wrote $8^2$ in full. Keep only its last digit.
You jumped ahead. 1 is the last digit of $9^2 = 81$.
You added the digits of 64. Keep only its last digit.

feedback.correct: The last digit of each square: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64.
feedback.generic: Think of the squares.

explain.text: The terms are the last digits of $1^2$ to $7^2$: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49. Next is $8^2 = 64$, so the term is 4. Check: the digits mirror round 5, so after 9 comes 4, then 1.

options.why: You kept the hundreds. Each term keeps only the last two digits.
You repeated the last gap of $-8$.
You halved 84. Each step doubles.

feedback.correct: Double, then keep only the last two digits.
feedback.generic: Double each term and compare.

explain.text: $2 \times 37 = 74$, $2 \times 74 = 148$ gives 48, $2 \times 48 = 96$, $192$ gives 92, $184$ gives 84. Next $2 \times 84 = 168$, so the term is 68. Check: every term is even after the first, as doubling requires.

items.title: Squares left out
items.question: What comes next? 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, ?

options.why: You skipped 11. Only the squares are left out.
You listed primes after 10. 4, 6 and 8 show the terms are not all prime.
You jumped past 16. Only 16 is skipped, not 11 to 15.

feedback.correct: Every whole number except the squares.
feedback.generic: Which numbers are missing?

explain.text: 1, 4 and 9 are missing: the squares. So every non-square appears, and after 10 comes 11. Check: the next gap is at 16.

items.title: Squared triangles
items.question: What comes next? 1, 9, 36, 100, 225, ?

options.why: You repeated the last gap of 125. The gaps are cubes, and $6^3 = 216$ comes next.
You squared 20. The roots 1, 3, 6, 10, 15 rise by 2, 3, 4, 5, so 21 comes next.
You doubled 225.

feedback.correct: Squares of 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21: the triangular numbers.
feedback.generic: Take the square root of each term.

explain.text: The roots are 1, 3, 6, 10 and 15, the triangular numbers. The next is 21, so the term is $21^2 = 441$. Check: the gaps 8, 27, 64, 125 are cubes, and $225 + 216 = 441$.

options.why: You added 9 again. 149 has digit sum 14, not 5.
230 qualifies, but 203 is smaller.
212 qualifies, but 203 is smaller.

feedback.correct: The numbers whose digits add to 5, in order.
feedback.generic: Add the digits of each term.

explain.text: Every term's digits add to 5, in order. After 140, no number up to 199 works, and 200 to 202 add to 2, 3 and 4. So the next is 203; check: $2 + 0 + 3 = 5$.

items.title: Ending in 3
items.question: What comes next? 3, 13, 23, 43, 53, 73, ?

options.why: You added 10. $93 = 3 \times 31$ is not prime.
103 qualifies, but 83 comes first.
79 is the next prime, but it ends in 9.

feedback.correct: The primes that end in 3.
feedback.generic: Why are 33 and 63 missing?

explain.text: 33 and 63 are missing because they are not prime: the terms are the primes ending in 3. After 73, 83 is prime, so it is next. Check: 83 has no factor up to 9.

items.title: Counting factors
items.question: What comes next? 1, 2, 2, 3, 2, 4, 2, ?

options.why: 8 is not prime. It has the factors 1, 2, 4 and 8.
You missed a factor of 8. It has four: 1, 2, 4, 8.
You counted a factor twice. 8 has four factors.

feedback.correct: The $n$th term counts the factors of $n$.
feedback.generic: What does 2 at every prime place suggest?

explain.text: The terms count the factors of 1, 2, 3, ...: 4 has three, 6 has four, and each prime has two. The eighth term counts the factors of 8: 1, 2, 4, 8, so it is 4. Check: $8 = 2^3$ has $3 + 1 = 4$ factors.

items.title: Powers of two inside
items.question: What comes next? 1, 2, 1, 4, 1, 2, 1, ?

options.why: You added the two terms before a 1. The terms are powers of 2.
You repeated 4. The eighth term is the largest power of 2 in 8.
You restarted the pattern. Place 8 is divisible by 8.

feedback.correct: The $n$th term is the largest power of 2 that divides $n$.
feedback.generic: Compare each term with its place.

explain.text: The terms are the largest powers of 2 dividing 1, 2, 3, ...: 2 for place 2, 4 for place 4, and 1 at odd places. Place 8 is divisible by 8, so the term is 8. Check: the pattern 1, 2, 1, 4, 1, 2, 1 then repeats with 16 at place 16.

options.why: You added the digits of 145. Add their squares.
You repeated the last gap of 56.
You squared 5 but not 4: $1 + 4 + 25$.

feedback.correct: Each term is the sum of the squares of the digits before.
feedback.generic: Square the digits of 16 and add them.

explain.text: $4^2 = 16$, then $1 + 36 = 37$, $9 + 49 = 58$, $25 + 64 = 89$, $64 + 81 = 145$. So the next term is $1 + 16 + 25 = 42$. Check: after 42 come 20, 4 and 16, so the loop returns.

items.title: Each to its own power
items.question: What comes next? 1, 4, 27, 256, 3125, ?

options.why: You kept the base at 5: that is $5^6$.
You kept the power at 5: that is $6^5$.
You raised 6 to the 7th power.

feedback.correct: The $n$th term is $n^n$.
feedback.generic: Write each term as a power.

items.title: A square factor
items.question: A factor of 36 is picked at random, each of its factors equally likely. What is the chance it is a perfect square?

options.why: You left out 1. It is a square and a factor.
You counted squares among all of 1 to 36. Only the 9 factors count.
You left out 1 and 36.

feedback.correct: 36 has 9 factors, and 1, 4, 9 and 36 are squares.
feedback.generic: List the factors of 36 first.

explain.text: The factors are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36, nine in all. The squares among them are 1, 4, 9 and 36, so $\tfrac49$. Check: a square factor is $2^a 3^b$ with $a, b$ each 0 or 2, which gives 4 of the $3 \times 3$ choices.

items.title: The same pair
items.question: Two traders each pick 2 of the same 4 stocks at random. What is the chance they pick the same pair?

options.why: That is the chance both pick one named pair.
You also needed the same order. A pair has no order.
You treated each stock as a separate $\tfrac14$ draw.

feedback.correct: There are $\binom42 = 6$ pairs; the second trader must match the first.
feedback.generic: Fix the first trader's pair. How many pairs could the second pick?

explain.text: There are $\binom42 = 6$ pairs, equally likely. Whatever the first picks, the second matches with chance $\tfrac16$. Check: of the $6 \times 6 = 36$ pairs of picks, 6 match.

items.title: A triangular number
items.question: A whole number from 1 to 20 is picked at random. What is the chance it is a triangular number: 1, 3, 6, 10 and so on?

options.why: You left out 1. It is the first triangular number.
You counted 21. It is past 20.
You counted the squares as well.

feedback.generic: Keep adding 2, 3, 4, ... to list the triangular numbers.

explain.text: The triangular numbers up to 20 are 1, 3, 6, 10 and 15, found by adding 2, 3, 4 and 5. That is $\tfrac{5}{20} = \tfrac14$. Check: the next is $15 + 6 = 21$, past 20.

items.title: Told it is big
items.question: A fair die is rolled. You are told it shows more than 2. What is the expected face?

options.why: You ignored the news. Only 3, 4, 5 and 6 remain.

feedback.correct: 3, 4, 5 and 6 remain, equally likely: mean $\tfrac92$.
feedback.generic: Keep only the faces the news allows, then average.

explain.text: Given more than 2, the faces 3, 4, 5 and 6 are equally likely. Their mean is $\tfrac{18}{4} = \tfrac92$. Check: $E[X \mid X > 2] = \tfrac{(3 + 4 + 5 + 6)/6}{4/6} = \tfrac92$.

items.title: In line on a board
items.question: Two different squares of an 8 by 8 board are picked at random. What is the chance they share a row or a column?

options.why: You counted only the row.
You divided by 64. The second square cannot be the first.
You counted the first square itself among the 15 in its row and column.

feedback.correct: 7 squares share the row and 7 the column, of 63 left.
feedback.generic: Fix the first square and count the second's options.

explain.text: Fix the first square. Of the 63 others, 7 share its row and 7 its column, so $\tfrac{14}{63} = \tfrac29$. Check: there are $8 \times 28 \times 2 = 448$ such pairs of $\binom{64}{2} = 2016$, and $\tfrac{448}{2016} = \tfrac29$.

items.title: Parallel edges
items.question: Two different edges of a cube are picked at random. What is the chance they are parallel?

options.why: You divided by 12. The second edge is one of the other 11.
You took 1 of the 3 directions. The second edge cannot be the first.
You counted each pair twice.

feedback.correct: Each edge has 3 parallel partners among the other 11.
feedback.generic: Fix the first edge. How many of the other 11 run the same way?

explain.text: A cube has 12 edges, 4 in each of 3 directions. Fix one edge: 3 of the other 11 are parallel, so $\tfrac{3}{11}$. Check: $3 \times \binom42 = 18$ parallel pairs of $\binom{12}{2} = 66$, and $\tfrac{18}{66} = \tfrac{3}{11}$.

items.title: Never two heads running
items.question: A fair coin is tossed 5 times. What is the chance that no two heads come in a row?

options.why: That is the chance some two heads do come in a row.
You treated the 4 neighbouring pairs as independent. They share tosses.
You counted only the rows with at most one head.

feedback.correct: The good rows number 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 for 1 to 5 tosses.
feedback.generic: Count good rows by how they end: in T, or in TH.

explain.text: A good row ends in T after a good row, or in TH after one. So the counts add like Fibonacci: 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, giving $\tfrac{13}{32}$. Check: 0 heads gives 1 row, 1 head 5, 2 heads 6 and 3 heads 1, which is 13.

items.title: Three corners of a hexagon
items.question: Three of the six corners of a regular hexagon are picked at random. What is the chance they form an equilateral triangle?

options.why: You found one of the two equilateral triangles.
That is the chance of a right angle: a triangle through opposite corners.
You counted each equilateral triangle twice.

feedback.correct: Alternate corners give 2 triangles of $\binom63 = 20$.
feedback.generic: Which sets of three corners are evenly spaced?

explain.text: Only alternate corners give an equilateral triangle, and there are 2 such sets. There are $\binom63 = 20$ sets, so $\tfrac{2}{20} = \tfrac{1}{10}$. Check: fix one corner; of the $\binom52 = 10$ pairs for the rest, one makes it equilateral.

items.title: Three in a line
items.question: Three of the nine squares of a 3 by 3 grid are picked at random. What is the chance they form a line: a row, a column or a diagonal?

options.why: You left out the two diagonals.
You counted ordered picks but only one order per line.
You counted each line twice.

feedback.correct: 8 lines among $\binom93 = 84$ sets of three.
feedback.generic: Count the lines, then the sets of three.

explain.text: There are 3 rows, 3 columns and 2 diagonals: 8 lines. There are $\binom93 = 84$ sets of three squares, so $\tfrac{8}{84} = \tfrac{2}{21}$. Check: in ordered picks, $8 \times 6 = 48$ of $9 \times 8 \times 7 = 504$ is $\tfrac{2}{21}$.

items.title: No neighbours side by side
items.question: The numbers 1, 2, 3 and 4 are put in a row in random order. What is the chance that no two numbers next to each other differ by 1?

options.why: You found 2413 but missed its reverse, 3142.
That is the chance some neighbours differ by 1.
You counted four rows. Only two work.

feedback.correct: Only 2413 and 3142 work: 2 of 24.
feedback.generic: Where can 1 and 4 go?

explain.text: 2 may touch only 4, and 3 may touch only 1, so 2 and 3 must sit at the ends. That forces 2413 or 3142, so $\tfrac{2}{24} = \tfrac{1}{12}$. Check: listing all 24 orders finds just these two.

items.title: Are the heads together
items.question: A fair coin is tossed 5 times and shows exactly 2 heads. What is the chance that the two heads are next to each other?

options.why: You did not use the news. Divide by the 10 rows with 2 heads, not by 32.
That is the chance they are apart.
That is the chance two given tosses are both heads. Two heads are already given.

feedback.correct: 4 of the 10 places for two heads are side by side.
feedback.generic: Given 2 heads, every choice of their two places is equally likely.

explain.text: Given exactly 2 heads, the $\binom52 = 10$ pairs of places are equally likely. Four are side by side, so $\tfrac{4}{10} = \tfrac25$. Check: $P(\text{together}) = \tfrac{4}{32}$ and $P(\text{2 heads}) = \tfrac{10}{32}$; their ratio is $\tfrac25$.

items.title: An even number of heads
items.question: A coin lands heads with chance $\tfrac13$. It is tossed 3 times. What is the chance of an even number of heads? (Zero counts as even.)

options.why: You treated the coin as fair.
That is the chance of an odd number of heads.
You counted only zero heads.

feedback.generic: Add the chances of 0 heads and of 2 heads.

explain.text: No heads: $(\tfrac23)^3 = \tfrac{8}{27}$. Two heads: $3 \times \tfrac19 \times \tfrac23 = \tfrac{6}{27}$. Together $\tfrac{14}{27}$; check: $\tfrac{1 + (1 - 2p)^3}{2} = \tfrac{1 + 1/27}{2} = \tfrac{14}{27}$.

items.title: Heads, given some
items.question: Three fair coins are tossed. You are told at least one shows heads. What is the expected number of heads?

options.why: You ignored the news.
You treated 1, 2 and 3 heads as equally likely. One head is three times as likely as three.
You multiplied by $\tfrac78$ instead of dividing.

feedback.generic: The case with no heads adds nothing to the mean. Remove its chance.

explain.text: The 7 rows with a head have $3 \times 1 + 3 \times 2 + 1 \times 3 = 12$ heads, so the mean is $\tfrac{12}{7}$. Check: $E[H] = \tfrac32$ and $P(H \ge 1) = \tfrac78$, and $\tfrac32 \div \tfrac78 = \tfrac{12}{7}$.

items.title: Told the larger card
items.question: Ten cards are numbered 1 to 10. Two are dealt. The larger number is 8. What is the chance the two numbers add to at least 12?

options.why: You did not use the news. Divide by the 7 pairs whose larger is 8.
You needed more than 12. A total of exactly 12 counts.
You let the smaller card be 8 as well.

feedback.correct: The smaller is 1 to 7, equally likely; 4 to 7 work.
feedback.generic: Given the larger is 8, what can the smaller be?

explain.text: Given the larger is 8, the smaller is any of 1 to 7, each equally likely. A total of at least 12 needs the smaller to be 4, 5, 6 or 7, so $\tfrac47$. Check: 4 of the 45 pairs qualify and 7 have larger 8, and $\tfrac{4}{45} \div \tfrac{7}{45} = \tfrac47$.

items.title: Only even rolls
items.question: A fair die is rolled until the first 6. You are told every roll was even. What is the expected number of rolls?

options.why: You treated the rolls as drawn from 2, 4 and 6 only. The news also rules out long runs, which shortens the wait.
You ignored the news.
That is the chance every roll is even, not the expected number of rolls.

feedback.correct: Stop at the first 1, 3, 5 or 6; given that it is a 6, the wait is unchanged at $\tfrac{6}{4}$.
feedback.generic: Each roll that is not 2 or 4 ends the story. Does knowing how it ended change when?

explain.text: Stopping at the first 1, 3, 5 or 6 takes $\tfrac64 = \tfrac32$ rolls on average. The news says that stop was a 6, and which face stops it does not depend on when. So the answer is $\tfrac32$; check: $\sum n (\tfrac13)^{n-1} \tfrac16 \div \tfrac14 = \tfrac32$.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: Two heads in a row somewhere in 3 tosses of a coin
A random factor of 12 is even
A random square of an 8 by 8 board lies on its edge

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.667, 0.438, 0.375.
feedback.generic: Overlapping windows share tosses, so do not add their chances.

explain.text: A random factor of 12 is even: 0.667. A random square of an 8 by 8 board lies on its edge: 0.438. Two heads in a row somewhere in 3 tosses of a coin: 0.375.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: Three heads in a row somewhere in 5 tosses
Two random squares of a 3 by 3 grid share a side
A random whole number from 10 to 99 has two equal digits

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.333, 0.250, 0.100.
feedback.generic: Count each event; do not add the chances of overlapping runs.

explain.text: Two random squares of a 3 by 3 grid share a side: 0.333. Three heads in a row somewhere in 5 tosses: 0.250. A random whole number from 10 to 99 has two equal digits: 0.100.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: Three random corners of a regular octagon form a right-angled triangle
Three heads in a row somewhere in 10 tosses
A random factor of 30 is prime

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.508, 0.429, 0.375.
feedback.generic: Eight windows of three tosses do not make a run certain.

explain.text: Three heads in a row somewhere in 10 tosses: 0.508. Three random corners of a regular octagon form a right-angled triangle: 0.429. A random factor of 30 is prime: 0.375.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: A random whole number from 1 to 20 contains the digit 1
Two different random numbers from 1 to 6 differ by 1
Two heads in a row somewhere in 6 tosses

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.672, 0.550, 0.333.
feedback.generic: Five windows of two tosses do not add to $\tfrac54$.

explain.text: Two heads in a row somewhere in 6 tosses: 0.672. A random whole number from 1 to 20 contains the digit 1: 0.550. Two different random numbers from 1 to 6 differ by 1: 0.333.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: Four heads in a row somewhere in 12 tosses
A random factor of 36 is odd
Three heads in a row somewhere in 7 tosses

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.367, 0.333, 0.299.
feedback.generic: Both runs tempt you to multiply windows by chances. Count instead.

explain.text: Three heads in a row somewhere in 7 tosses: 0.367. A random factor of 36 is odd: 0.333. Four heads in a row somewhere in 12 tosses: 0.299.

items.title: Rank three events
items.question: Put the three events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: Four heads in a row somewhere in 16 tosses
Two heads in a row somewhere in 4 tosses
Three heads in a row somewhere in 8 tosses

feedback.correct: Most likely first: 0.500, 0.418, 0.395.
feedback.generic: Do not assume the events tie because the windows times the chance match.

explain.text: Two heads in a row somewhere in 4 tosses: 0.500. Three heads in a row somewhere in 8 tosses: 0.418. Four heads in a row somewhere in 16 tosses: 0.395.

items.title: Shared seven ways
items.question: £1,000 is shared equally among 7 people. Choose the tightest interval that holds each share in pounds.

options.why: This holds the value, but 142 to 143 holds it too and is tighter. A wider interval scores less on the day.
This sits wholly below the value, 142.86.
This sits wholly above the value, 142.86.

feedback.correct: 142 to 143 holds the value, 142.86, and is the tightest that does.
feedback.generic: Bracket the value from both sides first, then pick the narrowest interval that holds it.

explain.text: $7 \times 142 = 994$ and $7 \times 143 = 1001$, so each share lies between £142 and £143. In fact it is £142.86. The interval 140 to 150 holds it too, but it is wider, so it scores less on the day.

items.title: Ten factorial
items.question: Choose the tightest interval that holds $10!$, in millions.

options.why: This holds the value, but 3.6 to 3.7 holds it too and is tighter. A wider interval scores less on the day.
This sits wholly below the value, 3.63.
This sits wholly above the value, 3.63.

feedback.correct: 3.6 to 3.7 holds the value, 3.63, and is the tightest that does.
feedback.generic: Bracket the value from both sides first, then pick the narrowest interval that holds it.

explain.text: $10! = 720 \times 5040$, since $6! = 720$ and $7 \times 8 \times 9 \times 10 = 5040$. That is 3,628,800, or 3.63 million. The interval 3 to 4 holds it too, but it is wider, so it scores less.

items.title: Ten reciprocals
items.question: Choose the tightest interval that holds $1 + \tfrac12 + \tfrac13 + \dots + \tfrac{1}{10}$.

options.why: This holds the value, but 2.9 to 3.0 holds it too and is tighter. A wider interval scores less on the day.
This sits wholly below the value, 2.93.
This sits wholly above the value, 2.93.

feedback.correct: 2.9 to 3.0 holds the value, 2.93, and is the tightest that does.
feedback.generic: Bracket the value from both sides first, then pick the narrowest interval that holds it.

explain.text: $1 + \tfrac12 + \tfrac13 + \tfrac14 = 2.083$, and $\tfrac15$ to $\tfrac{1}{10}$ add $0.2 + 0.167 + 0.143 + 0.125 + 0.111 + 0.1 = 0.846$. The total is 2.93. The interval 2.5 to 3.5 holds it too, but it is wider, so it scores less.

items.title: A late Fibonacci number
items.question: The Fibonacci numbers start 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, each the sum of the two before. Choose the tightest interval that holds the 25th.

options.why: This holds the value, but 75,000 to 76,000 holds it too and is tighter. A wider interval scores less on the day.
This sits wholly below the value, 75,025.
This sits wholly above the value, 75,025.

feedback.correct: 75,000 to 76,000 holds the value, 75,025, and is the tightest that does.
feedback.generic: Bracket the value from both sides first, then pick the narrowest interval that holds it.

explain.text: The 20th is 6,765, and each step multiplies by about 1.618, so five steps multiply by about 11.09. That gives about 75,000; adding on from 6,765 gives exactly 75,025. The interval 70,000 to 80,000 holds it too, but it is wider, so it scores less.

parts.name: I used no calculator
parts.detail: Tick this only if you sat all three papers without one.
